The Man with the Fear, Gustave Courbet, 1844

long: In his nightmarish self-portrait The Man Mad with Fear, Courbet looks out at us as a tense young man. His face and posture appear anxious and desperate.

His outstretched hand still seeks support, yet in the next moment the painter will plunge into a deep abyss. The dizzying threat of the scene is heightened by the unfinished, almost abstract foreground.

title: The Oraguay Rock, Maisières Valley, Doubs

image.alt: The Oraguay Rock, Maisières Valley, Doubs, Gustave Courbet, 1860

long: The rugged rock formations and river valleys of the region around Ornans are among Courbet’s preferred landscape motifs. Rather than documenting the topography exactly, he concentrates on the effect of space, light and material.
Through his vigorous use of the palette knife, the rock surfaces acquire a pronounced physicality, while more finely painted passages structure the surrounding landscape.
The small rowing figure and the unusual framing direct the viewer’s gaze toward the immediate experience of nature, conveyed above all through the presence of colour.

image.alt: The Manbouc Valley, Gustave Courbet, 1865/66

long: Only recently was the location of this landscape identified: the Manbouc Valley near Ornans, which Courbet often visited to paint. Yet he did not confine himself to depicting the limestone cliffs that define the landscape there.

Courbet also added a waterfall to the stream, flowing into a pool. In his paintings, the artist frequently applied a principle of montage, combining different landscape motifs from the area around Ornans.

title: [The Cour Napoléon Seen from the Tuileries, Louvre, Paris]
headline: Academy and Salon

image.alt: [The Cour Napoléon Seen from the Tuileries, Louvre, Paris], Édouard Baldus, 1852–1857

long: In nineteenth-century France, the Paris Academy and the Salon shaped artistic standards and careers. Courbet worked outside state training structures, yet remained both connected to these institutions and critical of them.

image.alt: The Stone Breakers, Gustave Courbet, 1849
Portrait of Charles Baudelaire, Gustave Courbet, 1848

long: In Paris, Gustave Courbet was well connected within circles of artists and writers. From 1847 onward, he was for a time linked by friendship with the Symbolist poet Charles Baudelaire.

In this painting, Courbet presents him as a cerebral bohemian, absorbed in reading and smoking a pipe in a sparse attic room. In 1855, Courbet incorporated the poet’s portrait as a quotation into his programmatic studio painting.

image.alt: The Apostle Jean Journet, Gustave Courbet, 1850

long: Since the 1830s, adherents of Fourierism, a utopian social philosophy based on the ideas of the early socialist Charles Fourier, had used lyric poetry and song to express their social ideals.

image.alt: After Dinner at Ornans, Gustave Courbet, 1849
image.credit: Original Source: bpk | GrandPalaisRmn | Philippe Bernard

long: In After Dinner at Ornans, Courbet transferred an everyday scene from his circle of friends into a monumental format traditionally reserved for historical or heroic subjects.

The depiction of a convivial gathering thus represented a deliberate challenge to academic hierarchies. The work provoked varied reactions — from sharp criticism to great admiration — and marked an important turning point in Courbet’s career.
The award at the Salon and the purchase by the state consolidated his artistic success.

title: Portrait of the Poet Pierre Dupont

image.alt: Portrait of the Poet Pierre Dupont, Gustave Courbet, 1868

long: Pierre Dupont belonged to the Parisian bohemian milieu and was closely connected with Gustave Courbet. The two met during the period in which Dupont was active in choral societies and in Parisian bohemian circles.
The republican-minded poet became known above all for his socially critical songs and shared central political convictions with Courbet and the social reformer Pierre-Joseph Proudhon.
In his portrait, Courbet dispenses with any form of social idealisation and presents Dupont as an authentic personality — far removed from the representative portraits favoured by bourgeois taste.

title: The German Huntsman
institution: Coll. Musée de Lons-le-Saunier, cliché Jean-Loup Mathieu

image.alt: The German Huntsman, Gustave Courbet, 1859
image.credit: Original Source: Coll. Musée de Lons-le-Saunier, cliché Jean-Loup Mathieu

long: Courbet’s hunting experiences in Germany were formative for him. During his stay in Frankfurt am Main in 1858/59, he took part in large hunts in the Taunus. Armed with a rifle, the “German Huntsman” approaches a recently killed stag with his hunting dog.
The model for this tightly cropped hunting scene was a photograph, which Courbet mentions in one of his letters.

image.alt: La vague (The Wave), Gustave Courbet, 1870

long: Courbet’s depictions of moving sea surfaces were already very popular during his lifetime and were later increasingly collected by museums in Germany.
Courbet paints the foaming, great waves and the dark clouds gathering in the sky. The painting demonstrates Courbet’s characteristic handling of paint with particular force:

Courbet’s energetic brushwork and palette-knife technique give the scene an immediate, dynamic force, making the sea’s power almost tangible. This painterly intensity helped secure his reputation as a forerunner of modern art.

image.alt: The Great Wave, Gustave Le Gray, 1856

long: At the same time, the seascapes also attest to Courbet’s engagement with contemporary photography, for example that of Gustave Le Gray.

image.alt: Coastal Landscape, Gustave Courbet, 1866

long: During his stays in Normandy, Courbet devoted himself intensively to painting the characteristic coastal landscapes. In 1866 he created this atmospheric picture with the white chalk cliffs of the Falaise d’Amont in Étretat.

The Source, Gustave Courbet, 1862
Jo, the Beautiful Irish Girl, Gustave Courbet, 1866

long: Joanna Hiffernan came from a lower-middle-class Irish family that moved from poverty-stricken Ireland to London in the early 1840s. There she gained access to bohemian and artistic circles.
In 1860, she met the painter James McNeill Whistler (1834–1903). In the autumn of 1865, Whistler, Hiffernan and Gustave Courbet came together for a working stay in Trouville.

The Source of the Lison, Gustave Courbet, c. 1864

long: In this painting, Courbet depicts the source of the Lison near Nans-sous-Sainte-Anne, focusing on the rough geology of the rock from which the river bursts forth before flowing into the Loue.
In doing so, Courbet brings the viewer’s gaze very close to the source.

image.alt: Courbet par Gill, André Gill, 1870

long: This work, not included in the exhibition, shows Courbet as a public figure. Here, he becomes the target of the caricaturist’s sharp pen in the weekly magazine “L’Eclipse” (Solar Eclipse)

André Gill depicts him in his full corpulence, with a pipe and painting tools. In his right hand, Courbet holds the red ribbon of the “Légion d’Honneur”. Courbet had rejected the honour in an open letter, citing his artistic independence
Only a short time later, the painter would become involved in the Paris Commune.

image.alt: Drawing: Paysage de l´Hérault, Gustave Courbet, around 1854

long: In Landscape of the Hérault, Courbet shows, among other things, the pines and cypresses growing there. The pencil drawing probably dates from one of his visits to Alfred Bruyas in Montpellier, around 1854 or 1857.

At Palavas, Courbet painted outdoors and created seascapes. Though marked by Mediterranean motifs — sea, ships and vegetation — the southern French landscape still reflects his preference for close, dark views of nature.

long: Courbet depicted Chillon Castle, situated on Lake Geneva, as an almost secluded structure surrounded by water.
